transcript.text: Let's start with your resume: you said you designed the ingestion API and Postgres schema for your document Q&A service — what were the main tables, and why did you split them that way?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: I started with fixed 500-character chunks and recall was bad for anything spanning a heading. I switched to splitting on headings first, then packing paragraphs up to 500 characters, and top-3 recall went from roughly half to about 85 percent on the 40 questions I had written down as a test set.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: That's a solid fix, cutting the miss rate by switching chunking strategy on real test data.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Now tell me about the Postgres schema itself — what were the main tables you designed for ingestion, and how did they relate?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: Postgres, one table for documents and one for chunks with a foreign key, and pgvector for the embeddings. I kept the embedding in the chunks table instead of a separate store because I only had 12000 rows and a join per query was cheaper than running a second service.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: That join-vs-service tradeoff makes sense at that scale.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Now walk me through the ingestion endpoint itself — what did a request and response look like, and what's one edge case, like a bad or duplicate upload, that you had to handle?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: Two endpoints. POST /documents took a file and returned a job id because ingestion took about 40 seconds and I did not want to hold the connection. GET /answer took a question and returned the answer plus the chunk ids it used, so students could check where it came from.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: That async job-id pattern for a 40-second ingestion is a good call.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Now tell me about something that actually broke in this project — what was your first guess at the cause, and what turned out to be the real problem?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: Ingestion silently produced empty chunks for scanned PDFs. I assumed the embedding model was the problem and wasted an evening on it. Then I printed the chunk lengths and they were all zero, so it was the text extractor, not the model. I added a length check that fails loudly on ingest.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: That's a good instinct, checking chunk lengths instead of guessing further.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: One last thing — running on a single VM with nginx and systemd, what happens if the process crashes at 2am, does it just stay down?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: I can speak to that. On the document Q&A project I made most of the backend calls myself, so ask me anything specific about it.

transcript.speaker: agent
transcript.text: Sure — specifically, does systemd restart the process automatically if it crashes, or would a student just see a dead site until you noticed?

transcript.speaker: candidate
transcript.text: On the Q and A service I owned the ingestion side end to end, so I can go into that.
